nameStory: Field chickweed gets its name from its love of open fields and meadows, where it spreads in low mats across the ground. The 'chickweed' part comes from the fact that chickens and other birds absolutely love to eat these nutritious little plants. Its other common name, 'mouse-ear chickweed,' refers to the small, fuzzy, oval leaves that look remarkably like tiny mouse ears!
description: Field chickweed is a low-growing perennial plant that forms spreading mats along the ground, rarely reaching more than 6 inches tall. It produces small white flowers with five deeply notched petals that look almost heart-shaped, giving the blooms a delicate, star-like appearance. The entire plant has a soft, fuzzy texture from tiny hairs covering the stems and leaves. This hardy little wildflower is part of the pink family, despite its white flowers.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white flowers with five deeply notched petals that appear almost split in half, creating a 10-petaled look. Each flower is about half an inch across and feels papery to the touch.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, oval leaves arranged in pairs along the stem, densely covered in soft, silvery hairs that feel velvety when rubbed between your fingers. They really do look like tiny mouse ears!

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading mats that hug the ground, with stems that trail along the surface and root at joints. The whole plant feels soft and cushiony underfoot.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces small, cylindrical seed capsules that split open at the tip like tiny brown lanterns, releasing numerous tiny seeds.

habitat: Field chickweed thrives in open, sunny areas with well-drained soil, including fields, meadows, roadsides, and disturbed ground. It particularly loves sandy or gravelly soils and can often be found growing in thin soil over rocks or in areas where other plants struggle. You'll often spot it in lawns, along path edges, and in areas with poor soil where its mat-forming habit gives it an advantage.

seasonality.spring: Begins producing its characteristic white flowers in late spring, with the soft, fuzzy leaves becoming more prominent as they emerge from winter dormancy.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with abundant white flowers appearing continuously through the warm months. The plant forms dense, green mats that are easily recognizable.
seasonality.fall: Continues blooming into early fall while beginning to set seed. The fuzzy leaves remain green and identifiable even as other plants begin to fade.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level in harsh winters, but the root system remains alive. In milder areas, some fuzzy leaves may persist through winter.

funFact: Despite being called 'field chickweed,' this plant is actually edible for humans too and has been used as a survival food for centuries - the leaves taste like a mild, slightly salty spinach and are packed with vitamins!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with common mouse-ear chickweed, but field chickweed has more deeply notched flower petals and tends to form denser, more cushion-like mats. Memory trick: Field chickweed flowers look more 'fancy' with their deeply split petals, fitting for a plant that prefers the 'fancier' well-drained field habitats.
contextualKnowledge: There's often confusion between the many 'chickweeds' - some are in the mouse-ear group (Cerastium) while others are 'true' chickweeds (Stellaria). The mouse-ear chickweeds are distinguished by their fuzzy, hairy texture, while true chickweeds are typically smooth and hairless.
compareHints: Field chickweed stands out from its mouse-ear relatives by forming the densest, most mat-like growth habit and having the most deeply notched flower petals. Common mouse-ear chickweed is more upright and weedy-looking, while snow-in-summer is much more silvery-white and ornamental. Field chickweed also tends to prefer better-drained soils than most of its relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its mouse-ear chickweed relatives, common mouse-ear chickweed is the most widespread and persistent in New England.
Snow-in-summer stands out dramatically from its mouse-ear chickweed relatives due to its distinctive 'tomentose' or felty white hairs covering the entire plant, giving it a silvery appearance.
Among the mouse-ear chickweeds in New England, sticky mouse-ear is the only one with that distinctive clammy, tacky feel from its glandular hairs.
American field chickweed differs from other Cerastium species by having the most deeply divided petals - they're split nearly to the base.
Among the mouse-ear chickweeds in New England, common mouse-ear chickweed is the most widespread and has the most consistently fuzzy texture throughout the plant.
Little mouse-ear is smaller and more delicate than common mouse-ear chickweed, which is perennial and has longer petals.
Unlike the very common mouse-ear chickweed which has fuzzy, spoon-shaped leaves and upright flowers, nodding chickweed has narrower leaves and distinctively drooping flowers.
Among its mouse-ear relatives, dwarf mouse-ear stands out for being the tiniest and having petals that don't extend beyond the sepals.
